title: "European Trade Network"
subtitle: "Centrality, communities, and resilience — CEPII BACI"
author: "Fatemeh"
date: today

## Overview

Countries as nodes, directed weighted trade flows as edges. Three questions: who is
central (and where does Austria sit), which trade communities emerge, and how resilient
is the network to losing its hubs. A fourth question treats energy (HS chapter 27) as a
separate market and asks whether it behaves like the rest of merchandise trade.

The short answer: the network is *complete* — every one of the 35 economies trades
directly with every other — so the interesting structure is not in which links exist but
in how lopsidedly value sits on them. That single fact shapes every result below.

![Bilateral merchandise flows, 2022. Node size is export strength; the strongest
corridors are drawn as arcs.](figures/headline/01_flow_map.png){#fig-flow}

## Data & method

- Source: **CEPII BACI** (HS17), year **2022**, aggregated from HS-6 products to
  bilateral country totals. Nodes: **EU-27 + 8 major partners** (GBR, CHE, NOR, USA,
  CHN, TUR, RUS, JPN) = **35 economies**, **1,190** directed edges, **9,755 bn USD**
  of trade.
- Directed weighted graph in NetworkX (edge i→j = exports from i to j in thousands of
  USD); DuckDB for node metrics, edges, community assignments, and the SQL rankings.
- **Betweenness needs a distance, not a capacity.** Trade value is a capacity, so the
  weighted betweenness below uses `distance = 1 / value_kusd`. Unweighted betweenness is
  reported too and is identically **zero** on a complete digraph — every pair is already
  adjacent, so no node ever sits on a shortest path.
- **Eigenvector and PageRank** use `value_kusd` directly as the weight.
- The graph is dense, so scale-free / small-world framing does not apply. Where a sparse
  object is needed — for community detection and for the resilience story — we extract
  the statistically significant **disparity-filter** backbone
  (Serrano, Boguñá & Vespignani, PNAS 2009) at α = 0.05, which keeps
  **184 of 1,190 edges**.
- Randomness (Louvain, random-failure runs, layouts) is seeded from
  `config.RANDOM_SEED = 42`.

::: {.callout-note}
2022 is the energy-crisis year and the first year of large-scale Russia sanctions. Values
are current USD, so the energy results in @sec-rq4 reflect prices as much as volumes.
:::

## RQ1 — Centrality and hubs {#sec-rq1}

**Germany holds the network together, and Austria does not bridge anything.**

Weighted betweenness is extraordinarily concentrated: Germany scores **0.829**, more than
four times China's **0.191**, with Italy third at **0.138**. Only **15 of 35** economies
have positive betweenness at all; the other 20 sit at exactly zero, because on a complete
graph a country is only "between" two others if the cheapest path between them detours
through it, and for most pairs the direct link is already the cheapest.

| Rank | Economy | Weighted betweenness | Exports (bn USD) | PageRank |
|-----:|---------|---------------------:|-----------------:|---------:|
| 1 | Germany | 0.829 | 1,354 | 0.124 |
| 2 | China | 0.191 | 1,654 | 0.069 |
| 3 | Italy | 0.138 | 507 | 0.053 |
| 4 | Spain | 0.059 | 321 | 0.038 |
| 5 | Greece | 0.059 | 37 | 0.011 |
| 9 | United States | 0.053 | 742 | 0.099 |

: Top economies by weighted betweenness. Note Greece and Lithuania (rank 6) entering the
top ten on tiny export volumes — betweenness rewards position, not size. {#tbl-centrality}

The gap between the betweenness and the volume ranking is the point. China exports *more*
than Germany (1,654 bn vs 1,354 bn USD) but scores a quarter of its betweenness: China is
a large source, Germany is a hub. Conversely Greece and Lithuania break into the top ten
on 37 bn USD of exports each, because they sit on cheap paths into the eastern
Mediterranean and the Baltic.

**Austria** is a mid-tier open economy with **zero betweenness**: 17th of 35 by export
strength (182 bn USD) and 13th by PageRank. It is not a bridge in the value-weighted
sense — its partners already trade with each other directly. Germany is its largest
partner on both sides (56.5 bn USD of Austrian exports, 82.5 bn of imports), followed by
Italy, then China on the import side and the USA on the export side.

The rich-club coefficient is **1.0** for every degree from 24 upward: the well-connected
economies are perfectly interconnected among themselves, which is what "density = 1"
means locally. @fig-backbone shows the network after the disparity filter strips it to
the 184 links that carry significantly more of a country's trade than a random allocation
would.

![The disparity-filter backbone: the 184 of 1,190 links that are statistically
significant at α = 0.05.](figures/headline/02_backbone_map.png){#fig-backbone}

## RQ2 — Trade communities {#sec-rq2}

**Three blocs emerge, and they follow geography rather than EU membership.**

Weighted Louvain runs on the undirected projection (i→j and j→i summed into one edge).
On the full dense graph the partition is weak — 3 communities at **Q = 0.151**. On the
backbone the same algorithm finds 3 communities at **Q = 0.252**, so that is the partition
we keep: moderate but real structure, which is about what a densely integrated trade
network should produce.

| # | Community | Size | Members | Exports (bn USD) |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| 0 | Continental core | 23 | DEU, NLD, ITA, FRA, BEL, ESP, POL, CHE, CZE, AUT, HUN, SVK, ROU, PRT, SVN, BGR, LTU, GRC, HRV, LVA, LUX, MLT, CYP | 5,237 |
| 1 | Extra-European partners | 7 | CHN, USA, JPN, RUS, GBR, IRL, TUR | 3,894 |
| 2 | Nordic-Baltic | 5 | NOR, SWE, DNK, FIN, EST | 624 |

: Louvain communities on the backbone, Q = 0.252. {#tbl-communities}

The EU-27 does **not** form a bloc — it splits across all three communities. The
boundaries are drawn by geography and trade intensity instead:

- Non-members **Switzerland** and **Norway** sit comfortably inside their neighbouring EU
  clusters (continental core and Nordic-Baltic respectively).
- EU-member **Ireland** defects to the extra-European bloc built around the US, China and
  the UK, because its exports are dominated by US-linked pharmaceuticals and tech.
- The **Nordic-Baltic** cluster holds together on regional intensity despite being split
  between EU members (SWE, DNK, FIN, EST) and a non-member (NOR).

Political membership is not what the flow structure encodes. Proximity and volume are.

![Economies coloured by Louvain community, sized by export strength, with the backbone
drawn faintly behind them.](figures/headline/03_community_map.png){#fig-communities}

## RQ3 — Resilience {#sec-rq3}

**Connectivity never breaks. Value breaks almost immediately.**

Economies are removed one at a time, tracking two things after every removal: the
**largest weakly-connected component** as a share of surviving economies, and the share
of the **original trade value** still carried inside that component. Targeted removal
takes hubs first — by out-strength, then by weighted betweenness, with both rankings
fixed on the intact network. Random failure is the mean of 20 seeded runs.

| Network | Strategy | Fragments at | Half of value gone at |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Full graph | random | never (100%) | 28.6% (10 economies) |
| Full graph | targeted (out-strength) | never (100%) | 8.6% (3) |
| Full graph | targeted (betweenness) | never (100%) | 8.6% (3) |
| Backbone | random | 88.6% (31) | 28.6% (10) |
| Backbone | targeted (out-strength) | 40.0% (14) | 5.7% (2) |
| Backbone | targeted (betweenness) | **34.3% (12)** | 5.7% (2) |

: Critical fractions. "Fragments" = the largest component no longer holds half the
surviving economies. {#tbl-resilience}

On the **full graph** the connectivity panel is flat at 100% by construction — a complete
digraph has no articulation point, so there is no bridge to cut and no trade agreement
could add redundancy that is not already there. That is a finding, not an artefact.

On the **backbone**, fragmentation becomes a real question and the answer is stark:
betweenness-targeted removal breaks it after **34% of economies (12 of 35)**, export-volume
targeting after **40% (14)**, against **89% (31)** under random failure. The network is
roughly **2.6× more tolerant of accidents than of a deliberate hit list**, and bridge
economies bite about two economies sooner than big exporters.

**Value is far more fragile than topology.** Removing China alone strands 25% of the
network's trade value; Germany alone strands 27%. Half of all trade value is gone once
**three economies (China, Germany, the USA — 9% of nodes)** are removed. Random failure
needs ten (29%) to do the same damage, making a targeted shock about **3.3× more
efficient** than an untargeted one.

The policy reading follows directly: stress-test the backbone rather than the full graph,
because shocks travel along the significant corridors; treat **diversification, not
redundancy**, as the lever, since the links already exist and it is the volume on them
that is concentrated; and watch bridge economies alongside big exporters, because
betweenness targeting fragments the backbone faster than volume targeting does.

For **Austria**, this means 4.0% of network trade value and zero betweenness — not a
chokepoint, and removing it changes nothing structurally. Its exposure runs the other
way: dependency on Germany and the other top hubs, not its own criticality.

![Resilience of the backbone: largest weakly-connected component (left) and retained
trade value (right), targeted vs random removal.](figures/headline/04_resilience.png){#fig-resilience}

## RQ4 — Energy subnetwork (HS-27) {#sec-rq4}

**Same 35 economies, same near-complete topology, a structurally more concentrated
market.**

Rebuilding the edge list with HS chapter 27 only (coal, crude, refined products, gas,
electricity) gives 1,146 links and **1,184 bn USD** — **12.1%** of merchandise value — at
density 0.96.

| Metric | All merchandise | Energy (HS-27) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Trade value (bn USD) | 9,755 | 1,184 |
| Links (density) | 1,190 (1.00) | 1,146 (0.96) |
| Largest exporter | CHN (17.0%) | RUS (23.4%) |
| Top 3 exporters | CHN, DEU, USA | RUS, NOR, USA |
| Top 3 export share | 38.4% | **54.6%** |
| Herfindahl index | 0.075 | **0.124** |
| Effective no. of exporters (1/HHI) | 13.4 | **8.0** |
| Austria export rank | 17 of 35 (1.9%) | 12 of 35 (0.9%) |
| Austria import rank | 15 of 35 (2.1%) | 18 of 35 (1.4%) |

: Energy vs total trade, computed identically on both graphs. {#tbl-energy}

The top three exporters carry **54.6%** of energy exports against **38.4%** for
merchandise overall — a Herfindahl index of 0.124 vs 0.075, i.e. **8 effective suppliers
instead of 13**. The leadership changes hands entirely: manufacturing hubs cannot sell
resources they do not have, so resource exporters replace them. Russia and Norway sit far
above the diagonal in the right-hand panel of @fig-energy; Germany and China well below
it. Once again the risk is concentration, not connectivity — the energy graph is nearly
complete, but the volume sits on very few sources.

**Austria** is 12th of 35 by energy exports (0.9%) and 18th by imports, a net importer of
5.5 bn USD. The ranking flatters it: Austria produces almost no fossil fuel, so its energy
exports are re-exports and transit — **53% electricity, 26% gas, 17% refined products**
passed on to neighbours. Its imports are equally intermediated, with **59% arriving via
Germany**, which is a routing fact rather than a production one.

Two caveats are part of the finding, not footnotes to it:

1. **The frame misses the real suppliers.** Only **48%** of this node set's energy imports
   originate inside it, against 65% for merchandise. Europe's crude and LNG largely come
   from outside the 35 economies modelled here — the Gulf, Kazakhstan, North and West
   Africa. This subgraph describes how energy is *redistributed* within Europe, not where
   it comes from.
2. **Pipeline gas is badly captured.** Austria's recorded HS-2711 imports inside the node
   set are 0.4 bn USD against 2.9 bn of exports, which would make it a net gas exporter in
   2022. It was not — it burned mostly Russian pipeline gas. Customs statistics attribute a
   flow to the declared consignment partner, so gas crossing hubs and traded contracts
   lands on the wrong edge. Read merchandise data as evidence about *value routed*, and use
   physical flow data for dependence.

**Bridge to the sibling project.** Electrical energy (HS-2716) is 9% of the energy
network's value but **53% of Austria's energy exports** and 35% of its imports — 5.9 bn
USD out against 5.7 bn in, an almost perfectly balanced position with Germany,
Switzerland, Hungary and Slovenia. That is the same physical flow that
[austria-energy-analysis](https://github.com/fatemeh-studio/austria-energy-analysis)
measures hourly from ENTSO-E. Read together, this project locates Austria in Europe's
energy exchange — mid-sized, intermediating, import-dependent — and the other explains
what the exchange is for.

![Left: cumulative export share down the exporter ranking (steeper = more concentrated).
Right: each economy's energy export share against its merchandise export
share.](figures/headline/05_energy_subnetwork.png){#fig-energy}

## Takeaways

1. **The European trade network has no structural weak point — it has a value weak
   point.** Every economy trades directly with every other, so nothing fragments by
   cutting links. But three economies carry half the value, and Germany alone carries 27%.
   Resilience policy that adds redundant connections is solving a problem this network does
   not have; diversifying volume away from the top handful of partners is the only lever
   that moves the number.

2. **Trade blocs are drawn by geography and intensity, not by treaty.** Louvain on the
   significant-trade backbone splits the EU-27 across all three communities it finds
   (Q = 0.252), places non-members Switzerland and Norway inside EU clusters, and sends
   EU-member Ireland into the US-led bloc. If you want to predict who trades with whom,
   distance and volume beat membership.

3. **Position and size are different things, and energy proves it twice.** Germany
   out-bridges China on a quarter of its export volume; Greece and Lithuania reach the
   betweenness top ten on 37 bn USD each. In energy the ranking inverts entirely —
   resource exporters replace manufacturing hubs, concentration nearly doubles
   (8 effective suppliers vs 13), and Austria rises five places on exports it does not
   produce but merely routes.
